title: The Women's March on Versailles, 1789 — bread, a palace and a king brought home
sources: Wikipedia: Women's March on Versailles — began among market women of Paris on the morning of 5 October 1789, rioting over the high price of bread; most workers spent nearly half their income on bread; a young woman struck a marching drum; many bore kitchen blades; the crowd converged on the Hôtel de Ville demanding bread and arms and ransacked it; thousands marched to Versailles in about six hours in the autumn rain, dragging cannons; the king received six women and arranged food from the royal stores; most of the crowd was not satisfied; at about six in the morning protesters found an unguarded gate and searched for the queen's bedchamber; the queen ran barefoot to the king's bedchamber and escaped; guards were killed; the crowd insisted the king return to Paris; on 6 October the throng — over sixty thousand — escorted the royal family back, guardsmen hoisting loaves of bread on their bayonets; at the Tuileries the king asked that a history of the deposed Charles I of England be brought from the library
Wikipedia: Charles I of England — executed in 1649; beheaded

Images (public domain / CC0 via Wikimedia Commons): 'À Versailles, à Versailles, 5 octobre 1789' (contemporary print); Valentine Prinsep, 'To Versailles' (painting, c. 1895); Janinet, 'Troisième évènement du 5 octobre 1789' (Hôtel de Ville, 1790); Caresme, 'Bravoure des femmes parisiennes' (1790s); 'Retour des dames de la Halle de Versailles le 6 octobre 1789'; Lafayette and Marie Antoinette on the balcony (18th-c. engraving); Callet, Louis XVI (1779); Vigée Le Brun, Marie Antoinette (1783); Van Dyck, Charles I (1632); Pierre-Denis Martin, Versailles (1722)

post.facebook:
On this day in 1789, the Women's March on Versailles began.

In Paris, bread cost most workers nearly half their income, and there wasn't enough of it. On the morning of 5 October, a young woman beat a drum in the markets; women armed with kitchen knives stormed the city hall, demanding bread and weapons.

Thousands then marched to Versailles through the autumn rain, dragging cannons. The king met six of the women and promised food — but most of the crowd did not believe him. At dawn, rioters broke into the palace and searched for the queen's bedroom; Marie Antoinette ran barefoot to the king's room and escaped.

The crowd wanted one thing: the king must come to Paris. On 6 October more than sixty thousand people escorted the royal family back, loaves of bread stuck on their bayonets.

In Paris, the king asked for a book from the library: a history of Charles I of England — the English king who was beheaded.
